title: Search Operators
summary: Use search-engine operators to narrow public web results.
learn: Operators let you constrain a normal web search by site, file type, URL text, title text, or exact phrases. Combine a few precise operators instead of building one enormous query.
notes: Use only public information and domains you are allowed to research.
when_to_use: Locating indexed pages within a known domain
limitations: Search-engine syntax differs by provider.
No result does not prove that a page or file does not exist.
Indexing can be stale or incomplete.
common_mistakes: Adding many constraints before testing a simpler query
Treating search results as a complete inventory
Assuming an indexed document is current

title: GitHub Search
summary: Search public repositories, code, issues, and commits for research clues.
learn: Start with a distinctive keyword, project name, domain, username, or error string. Narrow results with repository or language filters when appropriate.
notes: Do not search for or attempt to obtain credentials, secrets, or private data.
when_to_use: Tracing a distinctive error or package name
Finding public documentation and implementation clues
limitations: Public search does not expose private repository content.
A code match does not prove that the code is deployed or current.
Search indexes can lag behind repository changes.
common_mistakes: Treating a username as proof of identity
Copying an old result without checking commit history
Searching for or attempting to use credentials or secrets

title: Web Archives
summary: Compare older public versions of websites and documents.
learn: Archives can reveal how a public page changed over time. Record the capture date and compare meaningful changes rather than assuming an archived copy is current.
examples: Compare an old public press release with the current page
notes: Respect robots, site terms, and copyright. Archives are evidence, not automatically proof of current facts.
when_to_use: Verifying when a public statement or page was visible
limitations: Archives may miss assets or dynamic content.
Capture time is not necessarily publication time.
Archived pages are evidence of an observed snapshot, not automatic proof of every claim.
common_mistakes: Ignoring the capture timestamp
Assuming missing content was never published
Treating an archive snapshot as a live page

title: Reverse Image Search
summary: Use visual-search services to find possible sources, copies, or earlier appearances of a public image.
learn: Crop irrelevant borders when useful, try more than one search engine, and compare dates and surrounding context. A visual match alone does not prove origin.
examples: Search a distinctive crop containing the key subject
notes: Avoid using image matching to identify or track private people.
limitations: Search engines may not index every copy.
Resizing, cropping, compression, or edits can reduce matches.
A matching image does not establish who created it.
common_mistakes: Assuming the highest-ranked result is the original
Ignoring publication dates
Using image matching to identify or track private people

title: Metadata Basics
summary: Inspect metadata that is intentionally or accidentally present in files you are authorized to analyze.
learn: Images and documents can contain timestamps, software names, dimensions, and other metadata. Treat metadata as a clue because it can be removed or modified.
examples: Inspect EXIF fields in an image you own
Inspect document properties in a research dataset
notes: Do not use metadata to expose private location or personal information about someone.
limitations: Metadata can be stripped or modified.
Different tools write fields differently.
A timestamp in metadata is not automatically the publication timestamp.
common_mistakes: Treating metadata as immutable truth
Publishing private metadata unnecessarily
Inferring a person's location from metadata without a legitimate reason

title: DNS & RDAP
summary: Understand public domain-registration and DNS records.
learn: DNS can show public records such as A, AAAA, MX, NS, and TXT. RDAP can provide registration information where the registry makes it public.
notes: Public DNS information is not permission to probe or access the systems behind it.
when_to_use: Understanding a public domain's naming structure
Checking mail and authoritative DNS records
limitations: DNS answers can change and may be cached.
RDAP fields vary by registry and privacy policy.
A DNS record does not authorize access to the referenced system.
common_mistakes: Treating DNS as a complete asset inventory
Assuming an old record is still active
Turning passive discovery into unauthorized probing

title: Certificate Transparency
summary: Use public certificate logs to understand names that have appeared in TLS certificates.
learn: Certificate transparency logs can provide historical clues about hostnames associated with a domain. Validate every hostname independently.
examples: Compare historical certificate names over time
notes: Use results for passive research; do not turn hostname discovery into unauthorized scanning.
limitations: Certificates can contain names that are no longer active.
Wildcard certificates reduce hostname detail.
CT logs are historical evidence, not a live service inventory.
common_mistakes: Assuming every certificate name is an active host
Treating CT results as permission to scan
Ignoring certificate dates and issuers

title: Username Search
summary: Research a public handle across sites when the research context is legitimate.
learn: Treat a matching username as a lead, not an identity proof. Compare public profile details, dates, language, and links before concluding that accounts belong to the same entity.
notes: Do not use this technique to stalk, harass, or expose a private person.
when_to_use: Studying reuse of a distinctive handle
limitations: Handles are not unique identifiers.
Profiles can be renamed or deleted.
Public information can be misleading or outdated.
common_mistakes: Equating a matching username with the same person
Collecting unnecessary personal information
Using correlation for stalking or harassment

title: URL Analysis
summary: Break a public URL into host, path, query, fragment, and parameters to understand what it represents.
learn: Look for meaningful path segments, parameter names, tracking parameters, and redirects. Never assume a parameter is safe to modify on a live service.
notes: Prefer offline parsing when experimenting with URLs.
limitations: URL semantics are application-specific.
Redirect chains can change the final destination.
Parameter names alone do not reveal server-side behavior.
common_mistakes: Assuming every parameter can be safely modified
Confusing a URL path with a filesystem path
Following unknown redirects without checking the destination

title: Geolocation Clues
summary: Estimate a location from visible public clues without relying on private data.
learn: Use signs, road layouts, architecture, terrain, language, storefronts, shadows, and map imagery as separate clues. Prefer several independent clues before making a conclusion.
examples: Compare public street features with map imagery
notes: Do not use geolocation to locate a private person or facilitate harassment.
when_to_use: Comparing visible infrastructure with map data
limitations: Many visual features are shared across regions.
Map imagery can be outdated.
Low-resolution images can create false clues.
common_mistakes: Jumping to a location from one clue
Ignoring contradictory evidence
Using geolocation to locate a private person

title: Source Verification & Triangulation
summary: Test an OSINT claim against independent public sources and distinguish observation from inference.
learn: Triangulation compares independent evidence rather than counting copies of one source. Check provenance, publication time, primary documentation when available, and whether sources actually provide independent information. Record confidence explicitly.
when_to_use: Validating dates and public project claims

examples.title: Independent confirmation
examples.action: Compare a public announcement with official documentation and an archived snapshot.
examples.why: Different sources can provide statement, technical context, and historical timing.

examples.title: Contradiction check
examples.action: Record evidence supporting and contradicting a claim before concluding.
examples.why: Explicitly tracking contradictions reduces confirmation bias.

limitations: Multiple sites may copy one original source.
Primary sources can contain errors.
Lack of corroboration is not automatically disproof.
common_mistakes: Counting duplicate articles as independent evidence
Ignoring contradictory sources
Presenting inference as fact

title: Robots.txt & XML Sitemaps
summary: Read publicly exposed robots.txt and sitemap files to understand declared crawler guidance and published URL lists.
learn: robots.txt communicates crawler preferences and is not an access-control mechanism. XML sitemaps can enumerate URLs intended for search-engine discovery. Both can help explain public site structure but may be incomplete.
when_to_use: Finding published sections or canonical URLs

examples.title: Sitemap
examples.why: May contain URLs intended for search-engine discovery.

limitations: robots.txt is not a security boundary.
Sitemaps may omit pages or contain stale URLs.
Dynamic sites may expose structure elsewhere.
common_mistakes: Treating disallow rules as authorization barriers
Assuming a sitemap is complete
Requesting URLs that require authorization

title: Public API Documentation
summary: Use publicly documented API references and schemas to understand a service's published interface without attempting unauthorized access.
learn: Public API documentation can expose endpoints, parameters, authentication requirements, response schemas, rate limits, and versioning. Documentation describes an interface; it does not grant access to protected resources.

examples.title: OpenAPI schema
examples.action: Read a public OpenAPI schema published by a project.
examples.why: Schemas describe documented routes, parameters, and response structures.

examples.title: Version comparison
examples.action: Compare public API documentation for two released versions.
examples.why: Can reveal documented interface changes over time.

limitations: Documentation can lag behind implementation.
Authentication requirements still apply.
Undocumented behavior should not be tested without authorization.
common_mistakes: Treating documentation as permission
Assuming every documented endpoint is public
Ignoring version and rate-limit information
